answers: An escaped lion, a taunting crowd, and an ill-prepared first-response team came together in Kenya to cause what some are saying was the unnecessary, senseless death of the lion, the country's Star reports. Mohawk, a 13-year-old lion who was one of Nairobi National Park's most well-known creatures due to his trademark mane and rep as somewhat of a "ladies' lion," had escaped from an unfenced section of the park and ended up in the town of Isinya, where he was promptly surrounded by a jeering group of men, the Washington Post reports. Mohawk became upset by the noise and the growing crowd—Kenya Wildlife Service officials tell the AP about 400 had surrounded him—and lunged at a 27-year-old man, who was sent to the hospital with bruises and severe lacerations on his back. The wildlife service already had an animal management team on the scene, but those rangers had only rifles, not tranquilizers. After Mohawk pounced on the bystander, the rangers felt they couldn't wait for a second team on its way with tranqs—so they unleashed what the Star says was nine bullets, leaving the animal "roaring and writhing in pain" as he died. "If the rangers had the right equipment, this lion would not have died," a local resident tells the paper. "You can't keep a lion in the midst of people for so many hours without stressing it. We blame them for this heinous act." The shooting has prompted plenty of backlash on social media, including a #JusticeForMohawk hashtag, but the wildlife service says it had no choice once the lion started attacking humans. "This action was taken as a last resort after an escalation of the situation and a concern for public safety," the Kenya Wildlife Service says, per CNN. A bunch of lions have busted out of the park lately, driven by what conservationists say is the noise from development projects, including a highway being built through the park. (Same ending, different means for Cecil the lion.)

The lion had escaped from the park two days earlier due to a territorial dispute with another lion. It wandered into the Kajiado district, near Nairobi, where it was surrounded by a crowd of onlookers. The lion, known for its distinctive black mane resembling a Mohawk, was reportedly tormented by the crowd, who threw stones and took pictures. In a moment of aggression, Mohawk attacked a boda boda rider, causing serious injuries. 

In response, KWS rangers arrived and, due to the immediate threat to public safety, decided to shoot the lion. The decision was made after a second team with tranquilizers was en route, but the first team acted to prevent further harm. The incident sparked widespread outrage on social media, with many calling the killing brutal and unnecessary. Critics argued that tranquilizing the lion would have been a more humane option, and some blamed the KWS for not having the necessary equipment or protocols in place.

Mohawk was born in Nairobi National Park in 2003 and was a popular attraction for tourists. He was part of the King Fisher pride and was known for his calm demeanor and frequent presence with lionesses. His death has raised concerns about the management of wildlife in urban areas and the impact of infrastructure development on natural habitats.

The incident is part of a broader trend of lions escaping from parks in Kenya and South Africa. In South Africa, a lion named Sylvester escaped from Karoo National Park, prompting a debate over whether to kill or relocate the animal. Wildlife officials in South Africa initially considered killing Sylvester, but public outcry led to a reconsideration of options, including relocation or improved fencing. Sylvester had previously escaped from the park and was known for evading capture for over three weeks.

The cases of Mohawk and Sylvester highlight the growing tension between human safety and wildlife conservation. African lions, already classified as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, face threats from habitat loss, unregulated hunting, and human-wildlife conflict. In Kenya, the expansion of Nairobi and construction projects have encroached on the park’s boundaries, leading to increased lion strays
